title: How Trump's next tariffs could drive companies back to China
gist: US import sourcing responds to tariff DIFFERENTIALS between countries, not to tariff levels: a 20% China-only smartphone tariff in 2025 moved two-thirds of US smartphone imports to India within months, while equally high tariffs on Chinese and Indian clothing moved nothing. With the Supreme Court's February 2026 strike-down flattening tariffs across countries and a US-China Board of Trade contemplating lower tariffs on $30 billion of 'nonsensitive' Chinese goods, the next Section 301 round on 16 economies could invert the incentive and pull supply chains back into China.

insights.claim: The variable that determines whether supply chains leave or return to China is the product-level tariff differential between China and alternative source countries, not the absolute height of US tariffs on China.
insights.speaker: Chad P. Bown
insights.so_what: Track product-level China-vs-alternative tariff gaps rather than headline China tariff rates when forecasting reshoring/friendshoring winners; a rising China tariff with a rising Vietnam tariff is a non-event.
insights.quote: In the absence of a substantial tariff gap, China is often too competitive on cost for sourcing companies in America to ignore.

insights.claim: US smartphone import sourcing flipped from over 90 percent China as late as October 2024 (India just 6 percent) to nearly two-thirds from India by May 2025.
insights.speaker: Chad P. Bown
insights.so_what: Demonstrates supply chains can re-route within roughly six months when the tariff gap is wide enough — reshoring timelines assumed to take years are too pessimistic.
insights.quote: By May 2025, nearly two-thirds of US smartphone imports were arriving from India, up from only 6 percent as late as October of 2024.

insights.claim: The speed of the 2025 relocation depended on logistics and regulatory workarounds, not just factory capacity: Apple chartered six cargo planes in March 2025 to fly roughly 1.5 million iPhones (about $2 billion) from India to the US and got Chennai airport customs clearance cut to six hours from 30.
insights.speaker: Chad P. Bown
insights.so_what: Air-freight and customs throughput are the binding constraints in a tariff scramble — watch freight rates and port/airport clearance times as early indicators of a sourcing shift.

insights.claim: India's iPhone assembly base was not built in response to tariffs; Foxconn and Wistron had already created the alternative supply chain, with the 2022 Shanghai lockdown pushing Apple to accelerate it.
insights.speaker: Chad P. Bown
insights.so_what: Fast tariff-driven relocation is only possible where latent capacity already exists — categories without a pre-built alternative will not replicate the iPhone playbook.

insights.claim: The India relocation was not one-way: US smartphone imports from China suddenly and temporarily rose from September 2025 despite the 20 percent tariff, because Indian quality and delivery problems ahead of the iPhone 17 launch forced Apple to shift orders back to Foxconn in China.
insights.speaker: Chad P. Bown
insights.so_what: Execution risk in alternative geographies can override a 20-point tariff penalty around product launches — a recurring seasonal reversal risk for India-sourcing narratives.

insights.claim: Clothing tariffs on China rose by more than smartphone tariffs did in 2025, yet US clothing imports did not switch to India, because Trump's Liberation Day and August actions did not exempt Indian clothing.
insights.speaker: Chad P. Bown
insights.so_what: A clean natural experiment showing that raising China tariffs alone does not shift sourcing — a warning against modeling reshoring off China-tariff levels.

insights.claim: By October 2025 US tariffs on clothing from India exceeded those on clothing from China, and by end-2025 the China-versus-Vietnam and China-versus-Bangladesh tariff differential was basically unchanged from pre-Trump 2.0 levels.
insights.speaker: Chad P. Bown
insights.so_what: Apparel sourcing incentives were effectively untouched by two years of tariff drama — discount claims that Vietnam/Bangladesh apparel gained structural share from tariffs.
insights.quote: For clothing, there was little new tariff incentive in 2025 to move a supply chain out of China to these alternative destinations.

insights.claim: The Supreme Court struck down the country-specific IEEPA tariffs in February 2026, erasing both the China-over-India smartphone gap and the India-over-China clothing gap.
insights.speaker: Chad P. Bown
insights.so_what: The legal foundation of country-discriminatory tariffs is gone; new tariff architecture must be built on Section 122/301, which shapes how discriminatory it can be.
insights.locator: In February 2026, the Supreme Court struck down

insights.claim: After the February 2026 ruling the US moved to a relatively flat cross-country tariff structure: temporary 10 percent duties under Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974, replaced in July by 10.0-12.5 percent Section 301 forced-labor tariffs on America's top 60 trading partners, again exempting smartphones including from China.
insights.speaker: Chad P. Bown
insights.so_what: Smartphones are now tariff-exempt from every origin including China — removing the entire economic rationale for India assembly on tariff grounds.
insights.locator: Since then, the US has applied a relatively flat

insights.claim: Sourcing has stabilized rather than reversed so far: between March and June 2026 nearly 60 percent of US smartphone imports still came from India, a larger share than in the four months before the Court's decision, and clothing sourcing showed little change.
insights.speaker: Chad P. Bown
insights.so_what: Supply chains exhibit hysteresis — once relocated they do not snap back immediately, giving a lag between policy change and trade-flow reversal that can be traded.
insights.locator: US import sourcing for smartphones and clothing has stabilized

themes.theme: Board of Trade and the reversal risk

insights.claim: A US-China Board of Trade agreed by Trump and Xi Jinping at their May summit in Beijing contemplates $30 billion of US imports of 'nonsensitive' Chinese products, with USTR running a public comment process to build the list and stating it would be willing to lower tariffs on those goods.
insights.speaker: Chad P. Bown
insights.so_what: The $30 billion nonsensitive list is a concrete, comment-period-visible catalyst: companies in those product lines get a China cost advantage over other origins.
insights.locator: For certain nonsensitive products, increasing US imports

insights.claim: Cutting tariffs on Chinese 'nonsensitive' goods while leaving them on the same goods from other countries would directly incentivize companies to switch sourcing back to China — and USTR's Greer stayed noncommittal when pressed on whether Chinese goods could enter at a lower rate than identical goods from elsewhere.
insights.speaker: Chad P. Bown
insights.so_what: The administration's own trade deal contradicts its de-risking rhetoric; a negative China tariff differential is a live policy possibility, not a tail scenario.
insights.quote: the same goods coming in from other countries.
insights.locator: When pressed, Greer also remained noncommittal

insights.claim: China's government stated in July 2026 that the Trump administration committed to keeping any new US tariffs on China — inclusive of the 12.5 percent July forced-labor Section 301 tariff — at or below 20 percent.
insights.speaker: Chad P. Bown
insights.so_what: A stated 20 percent ceiling on China tariffs caps how wide the upcoming Section 301 excess-capacity differential can get, tilting the odds toward sourcing returning to China.

insights.claim: A new tariff round is expected on 16 economies including China and India following Section 301 investigations into excess capacity, and its outcome determines whether supply chains keep leaving China or return.
insights.speaker: Chad P. Bown
insights.so_what: The completion date and product-line detail of the excess-capacity Section 301 findings is the single most tradeable upcoming trade-policy event for supply chain positioning.

insights.claim: If the new tariffs prove more legally durable than the IEEPA measures the Supreme Court struck down, the resulting reduction in policy uncertainty could itself push companies to increase sourcing from China.
insights.speaker: Chad P. Bown
insights.so_what: Legal durability is an underrated second-order channel: a stable tariff regime lowers the option value of geographic diversification, favoring the lowest-cost producer.

insights.claim: US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer publicly warned in a July New York Times interview that companies which already moved sourcing out of China would be making a mistake to move it back, framing China reliance as high-risk.
insights.speaker: Chad P. Bown
insights.so_what: Official rhetoric and official tariff design are pointing in opposite directions — the gap is where policy surprise, and mispricing, lives.
insights.quote: They understand the high-risk nature of being super-reliant on China.
